title: Where things are
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: N-gen + upari / adhaḥ / samīpe / purataḥ / pṛṣṭhataḥ + N + asti

rules.text: The LOCATIVE ending alone does at, in and on. gṛhe is 'at home', vidyālaye is 'at school', pustakālaye is 'in the library'. There is no separate word anywhere in the line and nothing has been left out.

English cannot build any of those sentences without a preposition, so you will feel a gap and you will fill it. Do not fill it. The -e on the end of the noun is 'at', 'in' and 'on' at once, and any word you add is a word too many.

Position words are POSTPOSITIONS and they take a GENITIVE. pustakasya upari is 'of-the-book on-top'; gṛhasya samīpe is 'of-the-house near'. Moving the word to the back is the small half of the rule — the noun in front of it changing shape is the real one.

The locative is where something IS and M6's accusative is where something is GOING: gṛhe asti against gṛham gacchati. English hands you 'at' and 'to' as a signal; here the signal is the VERB, and the ending on the place follows it.
kutra asks with M2's grammar unchanged: pustakam kutra asti? No inversion, no do-support, nothing moves. The answer is the same line with atra or tatra standing in kutra's own place.
atra and tatra take no ending at all, exactly like M4's time words. A word that POINTS at a place does not decline; a word that NAMES one does. That is the whole difference between atra and gṛhe.

asti is M3's verb doing a third job. It was 'there is' and, with an 'of' word, the whole of 'have'; with a place in front of it, it is 'is at'. One verb, and the shape of the sentence around it decides which reading you get.
One ending, three English prepositions. Whether you say at, in or on in English depends on the shape of the thing you are talking about; Sanskrit never asks, and the locative is the same either way.

The postpositional phrase travels as one piece, and it normally stands in front of the thing it locates: gṛhasya samīpe vidyālayaḥ asti. Read it back to front — 'of-the-house near' — and the English appears.
This module writes one verb and no more. Everything that changed is in the nouns, and asti is enough to say where anything is — there is no 'to be located', no 'to stand', nothing extra to learn.

words.note: M1's neuter noun, in the naming shape a subject wears. It is the thing being located, so nothing on it changes.
M2's 'where', standing exactly where the answer will stand. It asked about going there; it asks about being there with no change at all.
M3's verb in its third job: with a place in the sentence it says where something is. One verb covers 'there is', 'have' and 'is at'.

sentences.trap: M2's question grammar, untouched by five modules. Nothing inverts, no helper appears, and the verb stays last — kutra simply occupies the slot the answer will occupy.
sentences.sound: PUS-ta-kam KU-tra AS-ti. The m of pustakam becomes a nasal hum in front of the k. kutra then runs into asti, its final a and the a of asti merging into one long aa — kutrāsti — and the page keeps the two words apart.

words.note: The 'of' shape of M1's pustakam. A postposition demands it: upari cannot stand behind the bare noun any more than English 'on' can stand behind nothing.
'On top of', and it comes AFTER what it governs. English puts 'on' first and leaves the noun alone; this comes last and puts the noun into the genitive.
The thing located, in its naming shape. The genitive belongs to the reference point, never to what is being placed.
'There is'. M3's existence reading and this module's location reading are the same word doing the same work.
